findings.summary: processStartOf runs `ps -o lstart=` in the local timezone, but the harness records procStart in UTC. Checked on the operator's machine (MST): registry procStart for pid 10996 is 'Tue Nov 24 23:59:58 2026', plain `ps` prints 'Tue Nov 24 16:59:58 2026', and `TZ=UTC ps` matches the registry. Result: on any host not set to UTC, resolveSessionSocket skips every registry entry and returns undefined. So (1) a stale-address send never repairs and always exits 1 with 'no longer resolves', defeating AC1 and the manual check in AC7; (2) a peer-name send always fails with 'does not resolve' (AC3); (3) see the next finding. Tests miss it because procStartOf is always stubbed. Fix: pass env {...process.env, TZ: 'UTC'} to execFileSync (or compare parsed Date values), and add a test that runs the real comparison against a UTC procStart.

findings.summary: pruneReceivedLog runs in `finally` on every `send`, successful ones included, and drops every named entry whose name does not resolve. Combined with the timezone mismatch above, any `cli-hierarchy send` on a non-UTC host rewrites every received-*.json to keep only unnamed entries. A follow-up `send --to uds:<live address>` then fails with 'not listed' until that peer messages again, which is worse than before this PR. Even after the timezone fix, the prune spawns one `ps` per named entry (up to 50 per log file) on every send, and its read-filter-write can race the hook's concurrent append. Consider pruning only the entry that just failed to resolve, or only on a failed send.

findings.summary: Acceptance criterion 4's test does not check the procStart comparison. The reused-pid entry (pid 7550, newest startedAt) has no messagingSocketPath, so its address comes out as uds:/tmp/cc-socks/7550.sock. The test's socketExists returns true only for custom.sock, so resolveSessionSocket skips that entry on the socket check alone. If the procStart line in send-resolve.ts were deleted, the test would still pass. Fix: make socketExists also return true for 'uds:/tmp/cc-socks/7550.sock' in this test, so the procStart mismatch is the only thing that rejects the entry. Optionally add a check that a matching procStart on the same entry is accepted.

Moving cleanup into try/finally or afterEach would prevent that.

findings.summary: The received log now keys entries by the `from-name` attribute. The cross-session-message tag is written by the harness host, and every party is a same-user local process, so this is not an exploitable boundary today. If a name could ever be set by another party, a forged name could drop a real peer's entry or redirect a repaired reply. A short comment saying the name is trusted only because the host writes it would keep that assumption visible.
